---
title: "3.5 — CDCL: learning from conflicts, and backjumping"
---

> **Where you are.** Slice 3.2's DPLL solves SAT by guessing and *chronologically* backtracking. That
> wastes enormous work: it can rediscover the same contradiction thousands of times in different
> branches. This slice builds **CDCL** — Conflict-Driven Clause Learning, the algorithm behind every
> competitive SAT solver since ~2001 — which, every time it hits a conflict, **learns a clause** that
> forbids the cause and **backjumps** straight past the irrelevant guesses. It's the single biggest idea
> in practical SAT. Code graduates into `Principia.Sat.Cdcl`.
>
> **Up front, honestly:** this solver is **unverified** — we do *not* prove it sound (the analysis is
> intricate). We justify it by **differential testing** against the *verified* `dpll` (the `#guard`s),
> and note that in practice its UNSAT answers are trusted via the **verified LRAT checker** of slice 3.6.
> "Fast untrusted solver + tiny verified checker" is the whole Course-3 thesis — and CDCL is the fast
> untrusted solver.

## 1. Why DPLL wastes work

DPLL backtracks *chronologically*: hit a dead end, undo the **most recent** guess, try its opposite.
Suppose variable `x₁` was guessed at the very top, and a contradiction only shows up after fifty more
guesses — all caused by `x₁`. DPLL will flip the 50th guess, fail again, flip the 49th, fail again… it
re-derives the same `x₁`-conflict over and over, never realising `x₁` was the culprit. CDCL fixes exactly
this: it figures out *which* assignments caused the conflict, records that as a new clause, and jumps back
to undo the real cause — skipping all the innocent guesses in between.

## 2. The trail and decision levels

CDCL tracks its assignment as a **trail** — a stack of assigned literals, each tagged with:

- the **decision level** it was set at (how many guesses deep), and
- its **reason**: the clause that *forced* it (a propagation), or `none` (a free guess, a *decision*).

```lean
structure TEntry where
  lit    : Lit            -- the assigned literal
  level  : Nat            -- decision level
  reason : Option Clause  -- the clause that forced it, or `none` for a decision
abbrev Trail := List TEntry      -- head = most recently assigned
```

A literal is **true** if it's on the trail, **false** if its negation is, **unassigned** otherwise — the
helpers `assignedTrue` / `isUnassigned`. Reasons turn the trail into an **implication graph**: each forced
literal points back, via its reason clause, to the literals that forced it. That graph is what conflict
analysis walks.

## 3. The loop: propagate, decide, conflict

Each round (`cdclLoop`):

1. **Propagate** (`bcp`). A clause is **unit** when all but one literal are false and one is unassigned —
   that one is *forced* true. Keep propagating units (recording each one's reason) until nothing is forced
   or a clause goes **conflict** (all literals false). This is the same `assign`/`clauseStatus` idea from
   slice 3.1, now reading the trail.
2. If propagation hits **no conflict**: if every variable is assigned, we have a model — **SAT**. Else
   **decide** a free variable (bump the level) and loop.
3. If propagation hits a **conflict** at decision level 0 (no guesses to blame): **UNSAT**.
4. Conflict at level > 0: **learn and backjump** (§4–§5), then loop.

You implement step-1's classifier, `clauseStatus` (§6); everything else is given.

## 4. Clause learning by 1-UIP

This is the heart. We have a **conflicting clause** (all its literals false). We want a *new* clause —
implied by the formula — that captures why, and that will become unit right after we backjump.

The trick: **resolve the conflict clause against the reasons of the literals it blames, newest first,
until only one literal remains at the current decision level.** That stopping point is the **first unique
implication point (1-UIP)**. Each resolution step is the very `resolvent` from Course 2 — so the learned
clause is a genuine *logical consequence* of the formula (that's why this is sound, even though we don't
prove it here).

```lean
def analyze (t : Trail) (d : Nat) : Nat → Clause → Clause
  | 0, learned => learned
  | fuel + 1, learned =>
    if (learned.filter (fun lit => decide (litLevel t lit = d))).length ≤ 1 then learned  -- 1-UIP reached
    else match t.find? (fun e => e.level = d && e.reason.isSome
                                 && learned.any (fun lit => decide (lit = e.lit.neg))) with
      | some e => match e.reason with
        | some r => analyze t d fuel (resolvent learned r e.lit.neg)    -- resolve away the newest blamed literal
        | none => learned
      | none => learned
```

**Worked example.** Decide `a` (level 1), `b` (level 2), `c` (level 3). Then unit propagation at level 3:

| clause | forces | reason |
|---|---|---|
| `¬c ∨ d` | `d` | `¬c ∨ d` |
| `¬a ∨ ¬d ∨ e` | `e` | `¬a ∨ ¬d ∨ e` |
| `¬b ∨ ¬e ∨ f` | `f` | `¬b ∨ ¬e ∨ f` |
| `¬e ∨ ¬f` | — | **conflict** (both `e`, `f` true) |

Start from the conflict `¬e ∨ ¬f`. Its level-3 literals are `¬e` and `¬f` (both `e`,`f` set at level 3) —
two, so resolve. Newest is `f`, reason `¬b ∨ ¬e ∨ f`; resolving on `f`:

`(¬e ∨ ¬f) ⊗ (¬b ∨ ¬e ∨ f)  =  ¬e ∨ ¬b`.

Now only **one** level-3 literal remains (`¬e`; `¬b` is from level 2) — that's the 1-UIP. **Learned
clause: `¬e ∨ ¬b`.** It says "you can't have both `e` and `b`" — a fact the original clauses implied but
never stated, distilled from this conflict.

## 5. Backjumping

Where to jump back to? To the **second-highest decision level in the learned clause** — here `¬b` sits at
level 2, so we backjump to **level 2** (undoing levels 3, discarding `c`, `d`, `e`, `f`). We pop the trail
to that level and add `¬e ∨ ¬b` to the clause set. Now, with `b` still true (level 2) and `e` unassigned,
`¬e ∨ ¬b` is **unit** — it immediately forces `¬e` (the *asserting literal*, the 1-UIP). So the backjump
isn't just undoing: it lands us with new propagation, having *learned* never to set `e` while `b` holds.

```lean
def backjumpLevel t d learned :=
  ((learned.filter (fun lit => litLevel t lit ≠ d)).map (litLevel t)).foldl Nat.max 0
```

When the learned clause's other literals span several lower levels, this can jump back **many** levels at
once — *non-chronological* backtracking. That's what saves DPLL's wasted work: CDCL undoes straight to the
real cause and never revisits the dead region.

## 6. Prove it

Everything is given except `clauseStatus`. Implement it (`make lab C=03-sat/04-cdcl`), and the differential
`#guard`s confirm your solver agrees with the verified `dpll`:

```lean
def clauseStatus (t : Trail) (c : Clause) : CStatus := …
```

- `.sat` if some literal is `assignedTrue`; otherwise look at the unassigned literals
  (`c.filter (isUnassigned t)`): none ⇒ `.conflict`, one ⇒ `.unit`, ≥2 ⇒ `.open_`.

§3 explains what each status means to the solver. Try it; §7 has hints.

## 7. Hints for the skeleton

*Nudge:* the four cases line up with: a true literal present; or the count of *unassigned* literals being
0, 1, or more. *More:*

```lean
def clauseStatus (t : Trail) (c : Clause) : CStatus :=
  if c.any (fun l => assignedTrue t l) then .sat
  else match c.filter (fun l => isUnassigned t l) with
    | []  => .conflict
    | [l] => .unit l
    | _   => .open_
```

If a `#guard` fails, your classifier disagrees with `dpll` somewhere — most likely the `.sat` check (a
satisfied clause must never be reported as conflict/unit) or the unit/conflict split.

## 8. Exercises (optional, for fluency)

1. **Trace the example.** On §4's clause set, hand-run CDCL: list the trail after the level-3
   propagations, identify the conflict, and reproduce the resolution `(¬e∨¬f) ⊗ (¬b∨¬e∨f) = ¬e∨¬b`. Which
   literal is the 1-UIP, and what level do we backjump to?
2. **Why these stopping rules?** Why does `analyze` stop at *one* literal at the current level (rather than
   resolving everything away), and why is the backjump target the *second*-highest level?

## 9. Corrections to the optional exercises

### Exercise 1 — tracing the example

After deciding `a,b,c` and propagating, the trail (most-recent first) is `f(3), e(3), d(3), c(3,dec),
b(2,dec), a(1,dec)`. The clause `¬e∨¬f` is conflicting (`e,f` both true). Resolving away the newest
level-3 literal `f` with its reason `¬b∨¬e∨f` cancels `f`/`¬f` and unions the rest: `¬e ∨ ¬b` (the two
`¬e` copies merge). Only `¬e` is now at level 3, so it's the **1-UIP**; `¬b` is at level 2, so we
**backjump to level 2**, where `¬e∨¬b` becomes unit and asserts `¬e`.

### Exercise 2 — the stopping rules

*One literal at the current level* is the definition of a unique implication point: every path from the
last decision to the conflict passes through that single literal, so negating it (asserting the UIP) is
enough to avoid the conflict — a maximally-useful, minimal-ish learned clause. Resolving *all* the way to
decisions instead would give the weaker "decision clause" (only chronological backjumps). *Second-highest
level* is the deepest level at which the learned clause is **unit**: every literal except the UIP is false
there, so backjumping further would lose propagations, and jumping less would re-enter the conflict
region. It's the exact level where the new clause does productive work.

## 10. Going further

- **Watched literals.** Real solvers don't rescan every clause to find units; each clause *watches* two
  literals and is only revisited when a watch becomes false — making `bcp` near-constant per propagation.
  Pure optimisation; behaviour is unchanged.
- **Restarts & VSIDS.** Periodically discard the trail (keeping learned clauses) and prefer to branch on
  variables involved in recent conflicts. These heuristics, plus clause learning, are what make modern
  solvers handle millions of variables.
- **The honest verification story.** This `cdcl` is unverified, validated here by differential testing.
  In production you don't trust it: it emits its learned-clause derivation as a **DRAT/LRAT proof**, and a
  *verified* checker (slice 3.6's `check_unsat`, or Lean core's `bv_decide`) re-validates the UNSAT —
  because every learned clause *is* a resolvent (§4), the proof is exactly a resolution derivation the
  checker can replay. Fast where speed is needed, verified where trust is needed.
- **Next: Course 4 — Euclid** (LeanEuclid + SMT), then **Course 5 — Gödel**.
